Print this page
This page applies to nationally significant infrastructure projects (
NSIPs
). It guides you through the design and consenting process to meet the biodiversity net gain (
BNG
) objective for
NSIPs
.
There is also
BNG
guidance for:
developers of sites that need planning permissions
land managers
local planning authorities
(
LPAs
)
When
BNG
applies to
NSIPs
From 2 November 2026, biodiversity net gain (
BNG
) will be mandatory for nationally significant infrastructure projects (
NSIPs
) in England.
NSIP
developers who apply for a development consent order (
DCO
) on or after this date need to deliver at least 10% net gain in biodiversity.
The statutory framework for mandatory
BNG
for
NSIPs
is introduced by
Schedule 15 to the Environment Act 2021
, which inserts Schedule 2A into the Planning Act 2008.
Mandatory
BNG
applies to
NSIPs
, or components of
NSIPs
, as far as the mean low-water mark, including the intertidal zone but not the marine environment beyond it.
Mandatory
BNG
does not apply to infrastructure consented through other routes, like Hybrid Bills.
Projects that cross England’s borders
Some
NSIPs
may cross England’s borders. The
BNG
baseline,
BNG
boundary plan and
BNG
metric calculation must only include habitats in England. Any biodiversity enhancements and creation that you intend to count towards your
BNG
must be delivered in England.
If you voluntarily choose to deliver
BNG
for any part of the project outside of England, you must calculate it separately. This will make it clear how the project will deliver mandatory
BNG
in England.
Follow the relevant biodiversity gain statement
In June 2026,
Defra
published
biodiversity gain statements for
NSIPs
. These explain how
NSIPs
need to calculate, deliver and report on
BNG
. They have the same effect as if they were included in the relevant
national policy statement
(
NPS
). The gain statements will be incorporated into the relevant
NPS
when each
NPS
is next reviewed.
You must follow the biodiversity gain statement relevant to your project to receive development consent. This guidance is supplementary to the gain statements and includes further information and best practice.
You will deliver
BNG
alongside existing environmental policies and obligations.
BNG
does not change or replace them.
The mitigation hierarchy
You should apply the mitigation hierarchy alongside
BNG
. This means avoiding significant harm to biodiversity in the first instance. Where this is not possible, you should minimise losses. As a last resort, you must provide compensation for any harm to biodiversity.
This is set out in the
gain statements
.
Check how
BNG
applies to irreplaceable habitat
You must follow the requirements set out in the relevant gain statement in relation to irreplaceable habitat.
There is further guidance on
how to treat irreplaceable habitat for
BNG
in support of these statements.
Measure biodiversity value
For the purposes of
BNG
, biodiversity value is measured in standardised biodiversity units.
A habitat will contain a number of biodiversity units, depending on things like its:
size
condition
location
type
To calculate the number of biodiversity units to achieve
BNG
, you must use the
statutory biodiversity metric tool
.
You must provide a single metric calculation for your development as part of your
DCO
application. This applies even where parts of the
NSIP
are not physically connected or are located in different local planning authority (
LPA
) areas. For example, where there is associated infrastructure or construction compounds separate from the main development.
This is also valid for phased development.
BNG
baseline
Using the metric tools and guides, you will need to calculate the biodiversity value of on-site habitats before development. This is called the
BNG
baseline.
The area on which you calculate the baseline is called the
BNG
boundary. This may not be the same as the development’s order limits. The order limits are the geographic limits of the powers the applicant is seeking through the
DCO
.
As the site layout develops during the design process, your
BNG
boundary may change. In that case, you will need to update your baseline.
What habitats to include in your
BNG
baseline
Your baseline calculation must include the pre-development biodiversity value of any habitats within your order limits that will be:
negatively impacted by the development
used to contribute towards the development’s
BNG
Habitats negatively impacted by the development
Your baseline must include all habitats within your order limits that will be negatively impacted by the development.
Your ecologist should advise on any expected negative impacts to habitats. This includes all habitats subject to permanent or temporary:
loss – for example, permanent loss due to development or temporary loss during construction
deterioration of habitat condition (based on the biodiversity metric condition assessment) – for example, from shading or disturbance caused by the development
You must consider all expected impacts, including those from:
development
enabling and site preparation works
construction activity, including direct habitat clearance, temporary compounds, storage areas and access routes
associated development included within the
DCO
application
expected impacts during the maintenance and operation of the development
On
Statutory biodiversity metric tools and guides
, you can find out how to:
conduct the habitat condition assessment – use the biodiversity metric condition assessments spreadsheet
record a deterioration in habitat condition – read the statutory biodiversity metric user guide
Impacted habitats that can count as retained
You can count habitats that are impacted temporarily as ‘retained’ in your baseline if you reinstate them to their original habitat type and condition:
within 5 years of the date the initial impact happened – for impacts on low or very low distinctiveness habitat
within 2 years of the date the initial impact happened – for impacts on medium distinctiveness habitat
If these conditions apply, you must still include these negatively impacted habitats in your calculation. However, you do not need to record them as lost. This reduces the number of biodiversity units you will need to provide for that habitat type.
The 2- or 5-year period starts from the date the particular habitat area is impacted. The date of impact, and therefore the end of the 2- or 5-year period, may vary for different habitat areas across the site.
There is more detail on accounting for temporary losses in the
metric user guide
.
If you intend to reinstate an impacted habitat within 2 or 5 years so that it can be counted as retained in the metric, but are subsequently unable to achieve this, you can no longer count it as retained. You must reflect this in your updated biodiversity metric and updated or phase gain plans.
Habitats used to contribute towards
BNG
As well as all negatively impacted habitats, your baseline calculation must include the pre-development biodiversity value of any habitats within the order limits that will be used to contribute towards
BNG
.
You should include any habitats where on-site biodiversity gains will be located. These are any habitats:
on which you plan to enhance or create new habitats
that count towards the post-development biodiversity value
You should include any habitats regardless of whether the habitat creation or enhancement is:
only for the purpose of
BNG
carried out for other purposes and you intend it to count towards
BNG
outcomes in part or full – for example, Environmental Impact Assessment mitigation or green infrastructure
To find out when habitat created or enhanced as part of your development for other purposes can also be used for
BNG
, read the guidance on
what you can count towards a development’s
BNG
.
If your project design details are uncertain
If the final project location or construction area is not fixed,
NSIPs
can include areas of design uncertainty or limits of deviation. You should determine the habitats to include in your baseline using professional judgement and the information available when you prepare your outline gain plan.
In your outline gain plan, you should describe:
the assumptions you have made
how you would address habitat impacts if an alternative realistic route is chosen
If you have uncertainty on the extent of habitat impacts
If you do not know the final extent of habitat impacts, your baseline must reflect the realistic worst-case extent of habitat loss or deterioration. This means using the maximum design and construction parameters for your project, rather than a hypothetical or overly precautionary scenario.
For example, for a linear scheme, you should use the maximum construction working width rather than the full width of the limits of deviation.
If you have uncertainty on the location of habitat impacts
Depending on the final location of your development within your order limits, you might impact habitats of different value, condition or distinctiveness. The approach you take to your baseline will depend on whether you have a most-likely route or design option, or not.
If you have a strongly preferred or most-likely route or design option, you should calculate your baseline using your realistic worst-case extent and that design option.
If you do not have a most-likely route, you should take a precautionary approach. You should assume impacts to the highest-value habitats that could realistically be affected unless you have mitigation, design measures or construction controls to avoid those impacts.
Scenarios: handling uncertainty about the location of impact
These scenarios show how you could apply the realistic worst-case approach where there is uncertainty about the location of impacts and which habitats will be impacted.
Each scenario is based on the construction of a linear project within the limits of deviation where no exact final route has been determined. They use the realistic worst-case extent of impact based on the maximum design and construction parameters for the project.
You may need to apply different elements of these scenarios across different parts of your project.
Scenario A: likely final route impacts habitats of high value
You have 2 possible routes:
a likely-final route: it impacts low distinctiveness grassland habitat, and a small area of high distinctiveness woodland habitat
an alternative route: it avoids the woodland habitat and impacts a larger area of grassland habitat instead – you are uncertain whether this route is viable
You take the following actions:
calculate your baseline using the most likely-final route, which includes the woodland habitat
in your outline gain plan, describe how you would account for additional grassland units if required – you do not provide extensive detail as grassland is a low-value habitat that is readily available in the off-site
BNG
market
Scenario B: 2 possible routes and high-value habitats on both
You have 2 possible routes, but no likely-final route:
route 1: it impacts a large area of woodland habitat (300 units over the total route)
route 2: it impacts a smaller area of wetland habitat (100 units over the total route)
You take the following actions:
calculate your baseline using route 1, which has the highest value based on the number of metric units
in your outline gain plan, describe the assumptions you have made
in your outline gain plan, describe how you would deliver any wetland units needed if you choose route 2
Scenario C: high-value habitats present but not expected to be impacted
You have 2 possible routes:
a likely-final route: it impacts only grassland
an alternative route: it impacts the same quantity of the same value grassland
There is an area of high distinctiveness wetland habitat within your limits of deviation, but this is not expected to be impacted by either route.
You take the following actions:
calculate your baseline using the likely-final route, not including the wetland habitat
design measures or processes to prevent impact to the wetland habitat throughout the construction and operation phases of the development
in your outline gain plan, describe these measures or processes
Unimpacted habitats
You can exclude unimpacted habitats from your baseline. You should only exclude these habitats if your ecologist can confirm that there are no expected impacts to them from the development. This includes permanent loss, temporary loss, or deterioration in condition.
You can also choose to include unimpacted habitats in your baseline. You might do this to:
simplify mapping and evidence
demonstrate the net gain across a larger area
If there are small parcels of unimpacted habitats, you should consider including them in your baseline. This will make your baseline more proportionate, easier to interpret, and simpler to evidence.
If you choose to include any unimpacted habitats in the baseline, they will be subject to the 10%
BNG
objective. These habitats will be included in the post-development biodiversity value and will count towards
BNG
.
Where infrastructure will be located above or below ground, the habitat beneath or above is usually included within the order limits. However, this habitat might remain unimpacted.
Below-ground infrastructure
For below-ground infrastructure or construction techniques, your baseline can exclude habitats above the works if you are certain they will not be impacted or degraded.
For example, if you use below-ground horizontal directional drilling, you may exclude areas of unimpacted habitat above the drilling area. You must include any habitats that will be impacted, for example during access, set up and working around the drilling access points.
Your ecologist should confirm that your working methods and impact avoidance measures will result in no impact to any areas you exclude from your baseline. They should consider the type of habitats present and the proposed disturbance depth.
Above-ground infrastructure
Your baseline can exclude areas of habitat beneath or immediately next to an above-ground structure if you are certain they will not be impacted or degraded.
For example, you can exclude habitats in the order limits beneath overhead electricity lines if you are sure they will remain unimpacted by the development. You must still include any habitats that will be impacted by site preparation or construction activity, such as habitats around pylons, access routes, or temporary storage areas.
Your ecologist should confirm that above-ground infrastructure will not negatively impact any habitats excluded from your baseline.
Survey data and baseline date
Get a professional to do a habitat survey
You should consult an ecologist with appropriate training and experience in habitat identification, creation and management.
They will need to survey the habitat before development and record the data needed for the metric calculation.
The baseline date
The baseline must use information that reflects the value of habitats on the date you submit your outline biodiversity gain plan.
The gain statements set out the requirements for the habitat survey, including:
appropriate timing, validity and updating of survey data
use of older surveys
You should consider using an earlier date in the following circumstances:
where unauthorised loss or impact to the biodiversity value of on-site habitat (‘degradation’) happened before you submitted the
DCO
application
if activities carried out under an existing planning permission or
DCO
that has not begun or has not been completed result in a lower biodiversity value of the on-site habitat than it would otherwise have been – for example, if a site is cleared under an existing planning permission, but the development is not built
The earlier date should be immediately before the degradation activities were carried out, or the closest date before this for which you have accurate data. This is to discourage the wilful degradation of existing on-site habitats to reduce the pre-development biodiversity value.
You should discuss the need for an earlier baseline date with the Planning Inspectorate as early as possible. The ‘examining authority’ (the inspectors who review your application) and the Secretary of State will then need to agree on your earlier baseline during the consent phase.
If you use an earlier date, you must have surveys or other evidence that show you meet these circumstances.
You do not need to:
account for any degradation before 30 January 2020
prove the absence of degradation since that date when submitting your
DCO
application
Making sure the survey data is accurate
Habitats on a site may change naturally over time or due to a change in habitat management. You need to consider whether the survey data is still relevant at the time you submit your outline biodiversity gain plan.
You will need to resurvey your site depending on:
whether the habitat type or condition is likely to have changed since your survey date
how long it has been since the date of your previous surveys
whether there have been any changes in the uses or management of the site
Your ecologist should help you understand if you need to update the surveys of your site. You should inform them if you know of any changes to the land use or management of the site.
Where survey data is unavailable
It may not be possible to access parts of the site or obtain accurate survey data, for example due to degradation. Where you do not have accurate data, you must calculate your baseline using any evidence or data available – for example, previous site surveys, online data sources and aerial imagery.
You should apply the highest-value type and condition of habitats that are likely to have been or be present on the site, based on available evidence.
Developing on an existing gain site
You must check if your development will impact:
a site that is already registered on the
national biodiversity gain sites register
any significant on-site gains that have been legally secured through another planning permission or
DCO
Considering
BNG
at an early stage in site selection and design can help you avoid impacting existing gain sites.
Where you cannot avoid impacts due to site constraints, you must calculate your baseline using the habitat type and condition the existing gain site is planned to achieve by the end of the 30-year management period.
The register lists all planned habitat for every registered gain site. You can use this information in your baseline calculation if your development impacts the entire registered gain site.
If your development impacts only part of a registered site, you will need to determine which planned habitats are within your
BNG
boundary. To work this out, you should take the following actions:
contact the owner, relevant
LPA
or responsible body of the site for detailed maps of planned habitats
check the
BNG
documents for the development the registered gains are allocated to
If you cannot obtain this, you should agree a proportionate approach with the decision maker considering the available evidence.
If significant on-site gains secured to another development are being impacted, you could look for the biodiversity gain plan or a habitat management and monitoring plan (
HMMP
) for that development on:
the local planning portal – for developments with planning permission
the
Planning Inspectorate
NSIP
portal
– for
NSIPs
If you cannot find detailed information in these sources, the relevant
LPA
where the site is located or the Planning Inspectorate may have this information.
If your development will impact existing gain sites, you may need to amend, compensate for or take on the legal agreements that are already in place. You should discuss this as early as possible with the signatories to the legal agreement and seek your own legal advice. The same measures apply if your development is on land that is already subject to other environmental or biodiversity-related legal obligations.
How to deliver
BNG
There are 3 ways you can achieve your 10%
BNG
.
For
NSIPs
, you can consider options 1 and 2 at the same time.
1. On-site gains
You can enhance and restore biodiversity on-site. For
NSIPs
, on-site means any areas within the
BNG
boundary.
All on-site habitat creation or enhancement is considered to be significant. You will need to consider early that significant on-site gains must be maintained and secured for 30 years.
Any habitat within the
BNG
boundary that you retain or will reinstate is considered non-significant. You do not need to secure it and can count towards your
BNG
. Reinstated habitats must be recreated to their original type and condition.
2. Off-site gains
For
NSIPs
, off-site means any habitat outside of the
BNG
boundary.
Any habitat within the order limits used for
BNG
purposes must be included in the
BNG
boundary. This means off-site habitats will also be outside the order limits.
You can make off-site gains by either:
creating off-site units on other land you own
buying off-site units from landowners on the off-site
BNG
market
Creating off-site gains on other land you own
If you own land outside your order limits, you can use it to enhance or create habitats. These can be allocated to your site.
To do this, you must follow the guidance for land managers for
creating off-site habitats
, including:
securing the gains with a 30-year legal agreement
registering the site on the biodiversity gain sites register
allocating the site to your development
3. Statutory biodiversity credits
This is a last resort option after you have exhausted all on-site and off-site opportunities.
If you want to buy statutory biodiversity credits, you must prove why you cannot meet
BNG
using on-site and off-site options.
Other work you can count as part of your
BNG
If you need to create or enhance habitats as part of your development for other purposes, you may be able to count all or part of this towards your
BNG
.
There is more information available on
what you can count towards a development’s
BNG
.
Plan your
BNG
delivery
You should consider
BNG
early as part of the overall project design. You will need to consider
BNG
alongside other environmental and planning requirements, as well as future uses of the site.
Each
NSIP
will have different constraints and opportunities that will determine how
BNG
can be delivered. The balance between delivering
BNG
on-site and off-site will vary between projects.
Design your
BNG
enhancement and creation
By taking an iterative approach and using the metric tool to test different design options, you can:
find the most efficient design that reduces negative impacts and avoids impacts to higher value habitats, where possible
refine your
BNG
design as wider project considerations become clearer
identify smart uses of
BNG
that can help to deliver other design benefits – for example, infrastructure resilience, social benefit, delivery of other environmental obligations and habitat connectivity
The most appropriate approach to delivering
BNG
will depend on a combination of factors including:
site characteristics
environmental context
project design and maintenance
wider project objectives – for example, climate resilience or the benefits to local communities
Ecological considerations
When designing any habitat creation and enhancement, you should make sure they are based on solid ecological expertise. They should take account of the ecological context of the change.
Consider whether:
the proposals are appropriate considering the use of the site, and the site surroundings – for example, if the habitat can withstand the expected levels of use where there is public access
the proposals will still be appropriate in 30 years’ time
soil conditions are suitable for your plans
plant species or habitat are suitable for the local area
there are light level or shade constraints
there will be suitable access to carry out management works – for example, for equipment such as mowers and hedge trimmers
You should also take into account the following conditions which could impact on your
BNG
plans, and consider how these might change over the 30-year management period for any significant gains:
climate resilience
geology and topography
agricultural land status
contaminated land
hydrology and drainage
flood risk zones
landscape character and designations
biosecurity
invasive plant species
These factors may influence:
the habitat type and condition that you can realistically achieve
the management required to establish and maintain it over time
Further details on how you can define and assess habitat condition are in the
statutory biodiversity metric condition assessment sheets
.
Deliver gains close to your development
Biodiversity gains may be delivered anywhere in England. You are incentivised to deliver on-site gains, or off-site gains close to your development. The metric tool applies a ‘spatial risk multiplier’ penalty to off-site gains that are located away from the development.
The spatial risk multiplier uses different boundaries depending on the type of biodiversity unit:
LPA
and National Character Area (
NCA
) boundaries for area habitat units and hedgerow units
Marine Plan Area (
MPA
) boundaries for intertidal units
waterbody and operational catchment boundaries for watercourse units
Off-site gains delivered in the same
LPA
,
NCA
or
MPA
boundary that your development is within do not incur a penalty and keep their full value.
Your
BNG
boundary may fall within multiple
LPAs
,
NCAs
or
MPAs
. In these cases, the multiplier is applied based on the entire
BNG
boundary, not on particular areas within it. This means you can allocate off-site gains from any of the
LPA
,
NCA
or
MPA
areas your
BNG
boundary spans without incurring a spatial risk multiplier penalty.
For off-site gains delivered further away in a neighbouring
LPA
,
NCA
or
MPA
, a penalty will apply. This will increase the amount of habitat required to achieve the same amount of biodiversity units. If off-site gains are delivered beyond these neighbouring areas, an even greater penalty will apply.
Deliver watercourse gains
Different rules apply to watercourse units. For watercourse units, the spatial risk multiplier is based on the specific waterbody catchment where the biodiversity loss occurs. This applies even when your
BNG
boundary crosses multiple waterbody catchments.
To incur no penalty, and keep their full value, you must deliver off-site watercourse gains within the same waterbody catchment where the biodiversity loss occurs.
A penalty will apply for off-site watercourse gains delivered outside the waterbody catchment but within the same operational catchment as the biodiversity loss. This will increase the amount of habitat required to achieve the same amount of biodiversity units. If off-site gains are delivered outside the operational catchment where the biodiversity loss occurs, an even greater penalty will apply.
Consider strategically important locations for gains
Biodiversity gains delivered as part of
NSIPs
can offer significant opportunities to help deliver wider nature recovery objectives in local areas, and contribute to benefits like:
habitat corridors that link existing areas of separated habitats – this could include existing or proposed gain sites
extending, buffering or linking existing statutory or non-statutory wildlife sites
supporting natural flood management
contributing to climate mitigation or adaptation
You should consider relevant
local nature recovery strategies
. These show proposals for nature recovery in locations where they will have the greatest impact (‘mapped measures’).
Through the metric tool, you can apply the strategic significance multiplier if you carry out habitat creation or enhancement that contributes to mapped measures. This incentivises the delivery of mapped measures as it increases the number of units generated. The
metric user guide
has detailed information on assigning strategic significance.
Timing of
BNG
delivery
If your project has long construction timescales or a phased delivery, you should consider when you plan to:
carry out habitat clearance on-site
deliver your biodiversity gains
The metric incentivises the delivery of habitat as early as possible, including before construction. It accounts for the time difference between biodiversity losses and compensation habitats being created or enhanced through the ‘advance or delay adjustment’. This adjustment can increase or decrease the biodiversity units you achieve.
Delivering habitats earlier can increase the units generated from the same habitat creation. This may be particularly relevant for linear or large phased projects where you may be able to deliver habitats early in parts of the site that will not be affected by construction activities.
Protected sites and species
BNG
does not change existing policy on protected sites and species.
If you are creating or enhancing habitats on a protected site or with protected species, you may be able to
count it towards your
BNG
.
Consider aerodrome safeguarding
Aircraft can be vulnerable to bird strike. This can pose a significant risk to aviation safety. 
There is usually a bird strike consultation zone around aerodromes. This can extend up to 13 kilometres from the aerodrome. If you plan to deliver
BNG
within a bird strike consultation zone, you must design and manage your habitats to avoid attracting birds that could increase the strike risk.
You should engage early with the relevant safeguarding authorities before you submit your
DCO
application. Relevant authorities may include:
the aerodrome operator
the Secretary of State for Defence – for military aerodromes
the Civil Aviation Authority
In your designs, you should:
demonstrate your
BNG
will not result in an unacceptable increase in bird strike risk
include appropriate avoidance, mitigation and long-term management measures
Considering safeguards early in your design process will help reduce the risk of issues arising during the project examination stage.
The Civil Aviation Authority provides further
guidance on wildlife hazard management
.
Calculate post-development
BNG
During your habitat design process, you must use the metric tool to calculate your post-development
BNG
value. This will tell you how much
BNG
you will deliver and if you will meet the 10% objective.
Your calculation must include any:
on-site gains
off-site gains – either that you intend to buy or from land you own
You must provide a single metric calculation and
BNG
boundary plan for your development as part of your outline biodiversity gain plan. This also applies if the project covers multiple
LPAs
,
NCAs
,
MPAs
, and waterbody catchments.
This is also valid for non-contiguous projects with separate areas of development within order limits, and phased developments.
You may have uncertainty about the planned creation or enhancement of some on-site habitat, particularly for later phases of large developments. Wider project uncertainties may also affect a specific area or phase of habitat creation.
If your
BNG
proposals are not finalised when you submit your outline gain plan, you will need to make assumptions about the enhancements you will likely make.
These assumptions will inform your calculation and the post-development biodiversity value. The value you will submit in the outline gain plan will set the expectations about the biodiversity value of on-site habitats. You will need to include the final value in the updated gain or phase plans.
Find off-site units
You can also deliver your
BNG
by allocating units from the off-site
BNG
market.
To explore the off-site market, you could:
search online – for example, on trading platforms
consult land agents, brokers or other consultants
speak with landowners or managers you already have links with
speak with your
LPAs
, who may sell or be able to signpost you to sellers in the market
speak with habitat bank operators
You can consider searching for a gain site that:
will create and enhance habitat to meet the needs of your specific
BNG
proposals
has already started creating and enhancing habitat that meets your
BNG
needs
You may require large numbers of units and habitat types that are more difficult to create. They may not already be available. You should engage with the off-site market as soon as possible to:
highlight your upcoming and likely future needs from the off-site market
allow off-site providers and habitat banks to plan and create the habitats that you need, in the location that you need them
give land managers a business case to proceed with more demanding habitat creation and reduce their investment risks
You do not have to buy units before you have consent for the project, but you can if you wish. You may wish to explore making flexible arrangements with off-site providers. This can help you demonstrate that you can deliver your
BNG
objective while allowing for changes as you go through the consenting process.
If you are buying from the off-site
BNG
market, you should:
follow your own procurement and due diligence procedures
seek your own legal advice on the sale with the providers
Estimate costs for statutory biodiversity credits
This option is a last resort if you cannot achieve on-site or off-site gains.
When you complete your metric calculation, the metric tool will show how many statutory credits you need to buy. The number of statutory credits depends on the number of remaining units you need to meet your 10%
BNG
.
Before you finalise your designs, you should
estimate the total cost of statutory biodiversity credits
you need.
Credit prices are set to incentivise developers to use the off-site
BNG
market. A spatial risk multiplier applies. You will need to buy 2 credits for every one unit you need.
Use or sell excess on-site gains
You can make on-site gains in excess of the mandatory 10%
BNG
. You may choose to do this, or it could happen because your project creates higher value or more habitats than needed. For example, grassland habitat beneath solar panels may be more valuable for biodiversity than the baseline habitat, and reservoir projects may create excess reservoir habitat units.
With your excess on-site gains, you can do one of the following:
allocate them to another of your own developments
sell them to another development on the off-site
BNG
market
keep the excess gains for your development
a combination of these
In all the relevant biodiversity gain plans, you must confirm whether you:
are keeping the excess gains for your own development
will make any or all of the excess available to another development
Allocate or sell excess on-site gains to another development
Excess on-site gains that you want to sell or allocate to another development must be treated as off-site gains for the other development.
This is a separate process from your
DCO
application.
You must meet all other requirements for making and selling off-site gains, including:
securing with a legal agreement – you may be able to secure your own on-site gains and the units you intend to allocate elsewhere in one legal agreement
registration on the biodiversity gain sites register
allocation to the other development
If you wish to sell and allocate, you should follow the
guidance for land managers
.
Keep excess on-site gains for your development
If you want to keep the excess gains for your development, and for this to be considered as part of your
DCO
application, these may need to be secured. Refer to the
relevant national policy statements
(
NPS
) or discuss with the Planning Inspectorate before submitting your
DCO
application.
Prepare your
DCO
application
Your
DCO
application needs to include:
an outline biodiversity gain plan
draft
DCO
requirements relevant to
BNG
Your
DCO
application will receive consent only if the Secretary of State is satisfied that you are able to meet the 10%
BNG
objective in line with the
relevant gain statement
.
Engage early with stakeholders
Engage early with the Planning Inspectorate and other relevant stakeholders. For example, local authorities, planning specialists, and public bodies with statutory responsibilities. This will help to inform your
DCO
application.
It is important to discuss:
the
BNG
objective for your project – as calculated by the metric
any need for an earlier baseline date to account for habitat degradation
the drafting of proposed
DCO
requirements, including if you propose to submit phase gain plans
the approach to discharging
DCO
requirements relating to
BNG
Plan to secure your gains
You must secure any significant on-site gains, off-site gains or statutory credits for them to count towards your
BNG
objective. You do not need to secure non-significant on-site habitats for them to count towards your
BNG
.
Securing your gains means creating a legal mechanism that requires you (or the person you buy the gains from) to:
undertake the planned habitat creation and enhancement works
maintain the habitats for at least 30 years
monitor the works and provide reports to the
LPA
or responsible body
It is also how you legally assign units to your development.
Secure significant on-site gains
You can secure significant on-site gains with:
your
DCO
requirements
planning obligation
(section 106) with an
LPA
conservation covenant agreement
with a responsible body
You must describe on-site gains in an
HMMP
. You must include your
HMMP
:
within your
DCO
application – if you are
securing any on-site gains through the
DCO
requirements
as part of your legal agreement
There is supporting
guidance on legal agreements for
NSIPs
.
The relevant decision maker may also require you to secure non-significant on-site habitats. For example, if locally important habitats are being retained or reinstated. Although they are not considered significant for the purposes of
BNG
, these habitats may be important for wider planning policy or contribute to locally important species.
Secure off-site gains and statutory credits
You secure off-site gains by
registering and allocating them to your development
. This applies whether you buy units on the off-site
BNG
market or if you create off-site units on other land you own.
You secure statutory credits by buying them. They must only be used as a last resort.
When to secure gains
You must include a schedule for securing any outstanding gains in your outline gain plan. This schedule should set out reasonable timeframes for securing gains for agreement with the decision maker.
You do not need to do this if you will have secured all your biodiversity gains by the time you receive development consent, for example, through your
DCO
requirements, planning obligations or conservation covenants.
You should take into account any uncertainty in your designs and schedule securing your gains throughout the process as you expect your designs to become sufficiently defined.
Once consent is granted, you will need to secure your gains in line with this schedule.
You should secure as many units as reasonably possible before development, or each phase of development, commences.
When you submit your updated or phase gain plans, you may be able to justify that it is reasonable to secure some units soon after development commences instead of before. For example, while you finalise an arrangement that would deliver better ecological outcomes or local benefits instead of buying units that are already registered.
You should only leave a shortfall of unsecured units where there is substantial uncertainty about the exact number or type of units that you need.
You must secure any remaining units before the project, or phase of project, starts operating (carrying out its function) at the latest.
Example: when to secure gains if there is design uncertainty
Your project is building a railway. You know it will impact woodland, but you do not know how much in total. That is because you do not know the exact route yet.
Because of your design uncertainty, you calculate parts of your baseline and design your
BNG
on a reasonable worst-case approach. In this worst case, you will need 23 woodland units.
Before you submit your updated gain plan, you secure the 16 off-site woodland units that you know you will need.
You schedule securing the rest of the gains after completion of construction when you will have certainty of the final impacts and the units you need.
After construction, you recalculate the gains you need. You determine you need a total of 21 woodland units. You secure 5 more units before your project starts operating.
Draft your
DCO
requirements
You must draft
DCO
requirements in line with the
relevant biodiversity gain statement
.
Secure the
BNG
objective
Your draft requirements must secure the
BNG
objective. They must secure that you will:
submit an updated or phase gain plans for approval after you receive consent
deliver
BNG
according to the approved outline gain plan and subsequent updated or phase gain plans
calculate any final shortfall in biodiversity units and secure any outstanding units before the project starts operating
Secure significant on-site gains with
DCO
requirements
You can also
secure significant on-site gains through a legal agreement
.
If you are securing significant on-site gains within your
DCO
application, your draft requirements will secure your on-site gains as described in the
HMMP
you submit with your
DCO
.
If the on-site gains that you secured with your draft
DCO
requirements change, you must update your
HMMP
and metric calculation, submit them with your updated gain plan and justify the change.
Your draft requirements must secure that you will:
submit an
HMMP
for approval with your updated biodiversity gain plan to the discharging authority before commencing the development
manage and maintain significant on-site gains for at least 30 years from the date the habitat enhancement works are finished
seek reapproval of an updated
HMMP
if there are any changes to the significant on-site gains allocated to the development
submit monitoring reports
Propose your discharging authority for
BNG
DCO
requirements are typically discharged by a relevant authority before work on much of the development can begin.
For
BNG
purposes, the discharging authority will have responsibility for approving:
updated biodiversity gain plans
any associated documents needed to secure
BNG
The discharging authority for
BNG
may be one of these:
the host
LPA
– when your site is within one
LPA
a lead
LPA
– if the project spans multiple authorities
the Secretary of State – particularly for complex, multi area projects
The choice should reflect the nature of the project, including:
the number of authorities involved
the expected technical complexity of the
BNG
proposals
the capacity of the relevant authorities to carry out the role
Before submitting your
DCO
application, you should discuss with the Planning Inspectorate and the relevant
LPAs
:
your intended discharging authority
the need for any consultation or coordination arrangements – especially if the Secretary of State or the lead
LPA
will act as the discharging authority
expected timings and the appeals process for discharging
DCO
requirements related to
BNG
These early discussions will help all parties to agree the approach. They will also reduce the risk of delays during examination or after consent.
You must name the chosen discharging authority in your
DCO
application, along with any other host or relevant
LPAs
to consult with.
Appeals mechanism for updated or phase gain plan refusal
You can include an appeals mechanism in your
DCO
application, as outlined in the planning guidance.
You should consider whether your proposed appeals mechanism will:
be suitable if the
LPA
refuses or fails to approve an updated biodiversity gain plan,
HMMP
, or other relevant
BNG
information
include an option for appeal if the
LPA
fails to make a decision in a specified timeframe
Create an outline gain plan
Your outline gain plan must include the details set out in the relevant gain statement.
This includes:
a strategy for meeting the
BNG
objective, whether on-site, off-site or through statutory credits
a schedule of timings for when you propose to allocate off-site gains to the development after consent
a description of any remaining uncertainty and how any changes to your
BNG
objective will be addressed
You will need to update your outline gain plan for approval from the discharging authority before you can start the development works. This approach gives flexibility for projects with evolving designs. It also makes sure
BNG
is secured at appropriate stages.
You will need to provide details and justification for any material changes between the approved outline gain plan and the updated or phase gain plans. The level of scrutiny for any changes should be proportionate to the significance of the change.
Outline gain plan for phased developments
If you are delivering your development in phases, you can submit biodiversity gain plans for approval on a phased approach.
You might wish to do this if the detailed designs of all phases are not known when you submit your
DCO
application.
Your outline gain plan must include:
BNG
proposals for the whole development site – this is because the examining authority will need to review if your overall plans will meet the 10%
BNG
objective
confirmation that you will submit detailed phase gain plans after consent
information about how each phase is expected to contribute towards the
BNG
objective
You may not have finalised the details of your proposals for some phases of the development. In this case, you should provide information on certainty levels for each phase and the assumptions you have made in your outline gain plan.
You must achieve 10%
BNG
for the entire development. The contribution of each phase towards the overall 10% will vary. If a later phase of the development does not go ahead, or is not completed, you must make sure that 10%
BNG
is still achieved for the development you have done. You may need to update your metric calculation and updated gain plans and secure any shortfall in units.
Provide evidence of what’s in your baseline
Your outline gain plan must include a
BNG
boundary plan. This must clearly show, and differentiate between:
negatively impacted habitat
areas of habitat that will be used to contribute towards
BNG
for your development
unimpacted habitats included in baseline
unimpacted habitats excluded from the baseline
Your
BNG
boundary plan must:
show the entire order limits, with the
BNG
boundary overlaid
be drawn to an identified scale
show the direction of north
have a clear legend showing the different categories of habitat listed above
If your baseline excludes areas of unimpacted habitat within the order limits, you should explain why or how the habitats will remain unimpacted in your outline biodiversity gain plan. You should also set out the assumptions or parameters you used.
For example, you could describe any measures you will use to prevent negative impact or provide evidence that construction will avoid the habitat area. This can include cross-referencing other application documents to avoid duplicating information, such as construction or works plans.
What to include in your outline gain plan when you have design uncertainty
If you have areas of design uncertainty when you submit your outline gain plan, you should clearly explain and justify:
your assumptions and design or construction parameters used to identify impacted habitats in your baseline
why they represent the most realistic worst-case approach
Where relevant, you should also describe:
any mitigation or avoidance measures you will use to prevent impacts
alternative habitat impacts that could arise under other realistic design or construction options
how you would secure additional biodiversity units if those alternative impacts occur
The level of detail should be proportionate to the value of the habitats, ease of habitat creation and availability of units in the off-site
BNG
market. If you do not end up impacting these higher-value habitats, you can update your calculation in your updated or phase gain plan to account for this.
Describe your off-site strategy
If you deliver any
BNG
off-site, you should demonstrate in your outline gain plan that you will be able to allocate the necessary units to your development after consent. You should include any:
evidence of unit availability
arrangements with habitat providers to reserve or secure units
agreements with habitat providers to create units you need
The evidence you choose to include should vary depending on your unit needs, the availability in the off-site market and how easy it is to create units for that habitat type.
If your outline gain plan does not provide sufficient assurance that you can buy the units you need, you are likely to face more scrutiny during the consenting process and risk delays.
Provide evidence of the need for statutory credits
If you think you will need to use statutory credits, you must include it in your outline gain plan.
You will also need to include justification that you intend to use them as a last resort because you cannot deliver all your
BNG
through on-site and off-site gains.
This evidence should show that you followed the relevant gain statement and the supporting guidance to:
consider
BNG
early in project development
engage early with the off-site
BNG
market
After you receive your development consent
Once your
DCO
application is approved, you will need to:
secure your units in line with the schedule in your outline gain plan – unless already secured with your
DCO
requirements
provide an updated or phase gain plans for approval to the discharging authority
Allocate off-site gains to your development
Once you have development consent, you can allocate units to your development, including those you may have bought earlier.
After consent, you may also need to buy and allocate more units if your metric calculation has changed or if you did not buy enough to meet your
BNG
objective before consent.
The land manager, or you with their permission, must
allocate the off-site units to your development
. This is done on the
biodiversity gain sites register
.
If the biodiversity gain site you have chosen is not yet registered, you can either apply to:
record the allocation of gains to your development
after the seller has
registered the gain site
record the allocation of gains to your development at the same time as applying to register the site
Before development can commence, you will need to have secured as many units as reasonably possible in line with the schedule agreed in your outline gain plan.
Buy statutory credits
If you are unable to deliver
BNG
through on-site and off-site options, you will need to
buy statutory credits
as a last resort.
Before you submit your updated or phase gain plans, you should begin the process of buying any statutory credits that you need. You will need to have finalised the purchase before you can commence development.
If you still have substantial uncertainty about the exact number or type of credits you need when you submit your updated or phase gain plans, you can buy any further statutory credits during or after construction. You must buy all required credits before the operation of the project starts.
Material or non-material changes to your
DCO
The mandatory 10%
BNG
objective does not apply specifically to
change applications
. However, the Secretary of State may consider any changes in your biodiversity value as a relevant and important matter when deciding the change application.
In your change application, you should provide information about whether and how the proposed change affects your development’s
BNG
objective. Where it does, you should set out how you will amend your
BNG
strategy so that you can continue to meet the objective.
Create your updated or phase gain plans
Your outline biodiversity gain plan will have provided preliminary evidence and information on your
BNG
proposals.
Before commencing your development, or each phase, you must submit an updated or phase biodiversity gain plan for approval from the discharging authority.
This plan will set out your final approach to delivering
BNG
, or
BNG
for the next phase, now that there is more certainty for the project or phase. It must:
implement the biodiversity objective as set out in the approved outline biodiversity gain plan
account for any updates to your development plans since you submitted your outline gain plan
amend the baseline date to the date you submit your updated gain plan to reflect the current site conditions
Your updated or phase gain plan must include all items listed in the
relevant biodiversity gain statement
. This includes:
an updated metric calculation – using an updated baseline date where needed
details and justification for any changes to on-site habitats, habitat impacts or development plans compared to the approved outline gain plan
an updated
HMMP
– if there have been changes to planned on-site habitats secured through requirements in the
DCO
supporting evidence for any changes – such as updated construction or works plans, engineering drawings, or details of impact prevention measures
an updated
BNG
boundary plan if there have been any changes, or confirmation that the original
BNG
boundary still applies
evidence of any biodiversity units that have already been secured (on-site or off-site) – including the biodiversity gain site register reference number
evidence of any statutory credits that have already been purchased
a strategy to secure any remaining biodiversity units or buy statutory credits and planned times
You should use version control to clearly label any updates to
BNG
boundary plans, metric calculation tools, and the supporting justification.
For phased developments, you must describe in detail what
BNG
proposals you:
have already done
plan to carry out as part of the current phase
will need to deliver over the remaining phases – you may still have uncertainty for later phases of the development
When to update your metric calculation
You must update your metric calculation, including your baseline where needed, if there will be a greater impact on biodiversity than you predicted in your outline gain plan. This could be because:
your updated development plans change the
BNG
boundary and result in a greater impact on habitats
changes you have made to your planned on-site
BNG
delivery result in greater impacts to habitats or lower provision of on-site
BNG
the value of existing on-site habitats being impacted has naturally increased with time
You may choose to update your calculation if, compared to the outline gain plan:
there are reduced impacts to habitats
the condition of any on-site habitats has naturally reduced
you will deliver more on-site gains than previously planned
Your updated or phase gain plan will need to include evidence of what has caused changes to the impact on habitats.
Baseline date for updated plans
For updated and phase gain plans, your baseline must reflect the site conditions on the date you submit your updated gain plan unless you used an earlier date in the outline gain plan.
Where you used an earlier date, the baseline date you use for your updated or phase gain plans will depend on the current habitat value compared to what you used in the outline gain plan. You should:
continue to use the earlier date for all current habitats of lower value
use the date you submit your updated or phase gain plan for all current habitats of higher value
The
gain statements
also cover special provisions for any degradation of habitat between submitting the
DCO
and any updated or phase gain plans. This includes activities permitted through your
DCO
that result in loss or negative impact to biodiversity.
In case of degradation, you should use an earlier baseline date. You should use one of the following:
the date immediately before the degradation activities were carried out
the closest date before degradation for which you have accurate data
If there is insufficient evidence about the biodiversity value of the on-site habitat immediately before the degradation, you can use the baseline date from your outline gain plan.
You should:
agree the earlier date with the discharging authority
include justification and evidence for the earlier date in your updated gain plan
When to resurvey for updated plans
The
gain statements
set out the requirements around survey validity for the updated or phase gain plans. They state that you can use the same survey data from the outline gain plan if your ecologists confirm that there have been no material changes to the habitats.
You will need to resurvey the relevant part, or all of the site, if:
there have been any material changes to habitat conditions
you had gaps in your survey for your outline gain plan, for example due to access constraints
Your ecologist should help you understand if you need to resurvey your site. You should inform them if you know of any changes to the land use or management of the site.
Appeal an updated or phase gain plan refusal
If you included an appeals mechanism in your
DCO
application, you can use this to appeal a decision of a discharging authority.
Before you can commence development
The development, or phase of development, cannot legally commence until all pre-commencement requirements in the
DCO
have been discharged.
Before the project starts operating
You must have finalised and secured the delivery of your
BNG
before you commence operation of the project. This means you must:
update the metric calculation if any additional impacts occurred during construction that have not already been accounted for – for example, where planned horizontal directional drilling was not possible
cover any shortfall in your
BNG
delivery – likely through the off-site
BNG
market or from statutory credits as a last resort
provide evidence that you have met your
BNG
objective to the discharging authority for their approval
For a phased project, you can commence operation when you have finalised and secured the
BNG
objective for that phase. You cannot commence operation of the final phase that you intend to build until you have finalised and secured the
BNG
requirement for the whole project.
You should still take these steps even if the development never operates.
Manage, monitor and report on gains
Significant on-site gains or off-site gains on other land you own
You are responsible for making sure the habitat is managed and monitored for at least 30 years. This starts when the habitat creation and enhancement works are complete, as defined in your legal agreement.
Your
HMMP
will set out what management, monitoring and reporting you must do. You are responsible for making sure that:
the management actions in your
HMMP
are delivered
monitoring surveys are carried out
monitoring reports are sent to the discharging authority
If you do not uphold your responsibilities from your
HMMP
, you might be in breach of your
DCO
or legal agreement. The discharging authority could take enforcement action against you.
If your development is going to operate longer than 30 years, you should continue to maintain the habitat for at least the whole period of operation.
If you buy off-site units
It is the landowner’s legal responsibility to make sure that the actions from the
HMMP
are undertaken. This includes managing, monitoring and reporting throughout the 30-year management period.
Case studies on the statutory biodiversity metric
Natural England provides
case studies demonstrating the use of the statutory biodiversity metric
. These are not specific to
NSIPs
, but examples on port development, river restoration and offshore wind cabling may be relevant.
Further information
The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) provides
NSIPs
guidance on:
national infrastructure planning
what to include in your draft
DCO
British Standards 8683 - Process for designing and implementing
BNG
, from the British Standards Institution. There is a cost to buy this for non-BSI members.

We will consider your feedback and update the guidance, where needed.

Details
The Product Safety Database (PSD) is the notification system used by local authority trading standards (environmental health in Northern Ireland), certain national regulators and Office for Product Safety and Standards (OPSS) enforcement teams to notify unsafe and non-compliant products to the Secretary of State, as required in product safety legislation. Unsafe products are those which pose a risk to the health and safety of consumers, whereas non-compliant products are those that do not conform to the relevant product safety legislation.
The information provides insight into the market surveillance activity of regulatory officers across the UK and highlights where the greatest levels of activity are taking place in terms of product sectors, as well as providing an oversight of the most reported harms and corrective actions taken.

Notes to the summary table
1. These data are provisional management information from live operational systems and are subject to change. The data have not gone through the same levels of quality assurance as official statistics.
2. These data are likely to include some duplicate records. As such they are a reflection of the information held in the system and may not be an exact record of the number of individuals who have been issued visas. Caution should therefore be exercised in using these figures.
3. Not all records of visas issued have a suitable postcode for mapping to upper or lower tier local authorities. The number of records excluded is about two per cent. Therefore these figures will not add up to the UK total published by the Home Office.
4. These data are the numbers of confirmed visa applications (noted as ‘visa applications received’ in Home Office publications), visas issued to come to or stay in England, Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland, and the number of persons that have arrived in the UK under the Homes for Ukraine Sponsorship Scheme, collated for operational purposes by the Home Office and Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. Total visa applications received are based on confirmed applications. This includes applications where the applicant has attended an appointment at a visa application centre and given their biometric information, or where the applicant did not have to go to a visa application centre to give their biometric information (which was possible from 15 March 2022). With effect from data provided by Home Office on 14 June, the figures in this release include information relating to applications where the applicant used the ‘UK Immigration: ID check’ app to prove their identity.
5. These data do not contain numbers of visas issued through the Ukraine Family Scheme.
6. There is a known undercount in the Northern Ireland ‘Arrivals into the UK’ data. This is due to people arriving into the Republic of Ireland and entering Northern Ireland via the Common Travel Area, where travel is not covered by the methods used to record entry to other parts of the UK. Ways to understand the scale of this undercount are being explored.
7. All data in this release have been assigned to local authorities or country based on the postcode of the sponsor’s address, or of the accommodation address if the applicant is not planning to stay at the sponsor’s address. The number of arrivals into the UK is therefore not necessarily reflective of the persons having arrived at the location noted in the table.
8. Some beneficiaries have indicated that either the Scottish Government or Welsh Government are their sponsor under the devolved government sponsor (also known as ‘super-sponsor’) element of the scheme. This is where Welsh and Scottish governments have undertaken to match beneficiaries without a named sponsor at the point of application, to a suitable sponsor in due course.
9. The Welsh government announced a temporary operational pause on new applications for their “super sponsor” scheme for Ukrainian refugees on 8 June 2022 with effect from 10 June 2022.
10. The Scottish government announced a temporary operational pause on new applications for their “super sponsor” scheme for Ukrainian refugees on 11 July 2022 with effect from 13 July 2022.
11. The numbers included in the tables include some visas issued where the ID numbers are not included in the list of visa applications received. The reasons for this are currently being investigated.
12. This information will usually be released at 9:30am on the final Thursday of each quarter.
Voluntary compliance with the Code of Practice for Statistics
The Code of Practice for Statistics was published by the UK Statistics Authority in February 2018 to set standards for organisations in producing and publishing official statistics and ensure that statistics serve the public good. Whilst the data from the Homes for Ukraine Sponsorship Scheme are not designated as official statistics, the principles of transparency of high-quality analytical outputs to inform decision making and the public underpin this data release: a
statement of compliance
is available at the ‘Voluntary compliance’ tab of the spreadsheet of tables.

Details
The annual autumn snapshot is our official and most robust measure of rough sleeping on a single night given they are independently verified, it provides information about the estimated number of people sleeping rough on a single night between 1 October and 30 November each year and some basic demographics details (age, gender, nationality). These statistics provide a way of estimating the number of people sleeping rough across England on a single night and assessing change over time.
In May 2023, the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government launched a new framework with a new set of metrics to better understand how far rough sleeping is prevented wherever possible, and where it does occur, if it is rare, brief, and non-recurring. This was developed with
Centre for Homelessness Impact
and 5 pilot areas (London, Greater Manchester, Newcastle, West Midlands and Bournemouth, Christchurch, and Poole). The information in the release is management information not official statistics.
We welcome users to contact
RoughSleepingStatistics@communities.gov.uk
if you have any feedback or comments.

Details
Local Plans Examinations data
We are currently reviewing the way we publish data in the Casework Database. The database previously included data on Local Plans Examinations casework. These data were incomplete and did not easily fit into the format of the database, which is designed primarily around Appeals casework. Moreover, most of the Local Plans-related information contained within the database is already available elsewhere in the publications found at
Local plans: monitoring progress - GOV.UK
(see tables “Plans containing strategic policies” and “Plans containing non-strategic policies”). As a result, we have taken the decision to remove the Local Plans Examinations data from the Casework Database. We are considering what data should be included to provide a more helpful publication on Local Plans Examinations casework in future. We would appreciate all feedback on this.
Unable to find what you are looking for?
If there is any Local Plans Examinations-related information that you would have previously found in the Casework database, that you cannot find at
Local plans: monitoring progress - GOV.UK
, please email us at
statistics@planninginspectorate.gov.uk
and we will be happy to provide this information.
Do you have requirements or suggestions for Local Plans Examinations data?
We are looking for ways to improve our data presentation. If you have any suggestions or particular requirements for future data releases relating to Local Plans Examinations, please let us know at
statistics@planninginspectorate.gov.uk
.
Updates
11 June 2025 update: A data processing issue has been identified, where the names of Inspectors involved in Local Plan cases were incorrect. This caused incorrect data for these cases, in previous versions of the casework database.
This has now been corrected and the names are now fixed. We are not aware of any other case types identified by this issue but will assess this in due course. If you have any questions about this please contact us at
statistics@planninginspectorate.gov.uk
27 May 2025 update: There has been a data processing issue with Tree Replacement Notices (TRN) were they were being incorrectly labelled as Tree Preservation Order (TPO). This has now been corrected and the labelling is now fixed.
03 December 2024 update: We have discovered a data quality issue with the number of residences field. We are investigating this issue and advise caution is needed when using this field. Linked to this, we have discovered some inconsistencies with the major housing development and minor housing development. This is being investigated, and we will provide updates as we can.
We have made corrections to our data on decision dates for Tree Preservation Order (TPO) cases since the previous database release.
In previous releases of the database, cases belonging to Somerset, North Yorkshire or Cumbria were incorrectly flagged as No LPA Associated. This has been corrected in the current database release.
24 May 2024 update: We have returned inspector name to the database but advise there are still blank entries where the decision maker should be known. We have made some improvements to data quality but further investigations and changes are still in progress.
29 January 2024 update:  There has been a data entry issue with Tree Preservation Order (TPO) cases where incorrect valid dates have been entered. This means we have removed the dates from this field for TPO cases.
If you have any questions on this please contact
statistics@planninginspectorate.gov.uk
.
12 June 2023 update: We apologise that due to a data processing issue, agents’ names are missing from casework decided after 31st March 2022.  This means it is not possible to say, for these cases, whether an agent was involved.
We are exploring this issue and will provide the missing names as soon as we can.
This data set includes detailed information on a selection of the Planning Inspectorate’s (PINS) casework decisions over a 5-year rolling period. Casework currently in progress and those which have been withdrawn or turned away are not included.
The number of appeals listed in the Casework Database may not match exactly with other Statistics published by the Planning Inspectorate, for example our Official Statistics that we publish each month.  This is due in part because the database and the Official Statistics were compiled on different days and that the data may have been updated in the intervening period.
We are looking into the possibilities for improving the publication of the Casework Database. If you would like to contact us about this, please do so by contacting
statistics@planninginspectorate.gov.uk
In 2021 we removed the ‘Development or Allegation’ field in the Casework Database. A review found an unacceptable risk that the field could contain, and disclose, sensitive personal data. We take data protection very seriously and this action has been taken to ensure we comply with the UK General Data Protection Requirement (Data Protection Act 2018).
We have expanded the casework database to include the following specialist casework types:
Common Land
Community Infrastructure Levy
Environmental
Hedgerow
High Hedges
Purchase Notices
Rights of Way (including schedule 14 and Rights of Way modifications)
Tree Preservation Orders
Older Casework Database
The Older Casework Data gives details of appeals that have a decision date between 5 and 10 years ago. The database will allow users to compile summary statistics. Due to data retention policy we have removed all fields that could make an individual appeal, which was decided more than 5 years ago, identifiable. This is in line with the Appeals Casework Portal which does not have details of appeals decided more than 5 years ago.
Therefore, unlike the Casework Database, we do not record in the Older Casework data:
Case Number
LPAs Reference
Name of Appellant
Name of Agent
Site Address
The Older Casework Data Reference Number is used in connection with the Older Casework data only. It is not connected in any way with the Appeal Reference Number or the LPAs Reference, or with the reference number in any previous or future Older Casework Data set.
We record the first part of the site address Post code on the Older Casework Data.
The casework types recorded in the Older Casework database are the same as those in the Casework Database.
If you want information about appeals decided in the last 5 years please see our Casework Database.
Please Note
This dataset is drawn from Planning Inspectorate admin systems. There are some fields which have been left empty for particular appeals. There could be various reasons for this, for example:
the relevant information was not provided by the main parties
the relevant information was a negative reply and the respective field was left empty. E.g. The site is not in a SSSI
the case is a child case and the relevant information has been recorded against the lead appeal
We are looking at ways to make this database as complete as we can. If you need any help or advice in interpreting the database please let us know.
We have various mechanisms for checking our data and being alerted to changes - therefore data can change between different publications of this data set. If you spot a data error please tell us;
statistics@planninginspectorate.gov.uk
.
Please note that the Planning Inspectorate will not entertain a challenge to the appointment of any Decision Maker on the basis of this data.
all cases are considered on their individual merits, and on the basis of the evidence submitted
targets are not set for the percentage of allowed and dismissed cases
decision Makers do not select their own casework
casework is allocated to Decision Maker on the best balance of availability, geography, casework level and expertise. This may produce apparent patterns of outcome that are in fact artefacts of the way work is allocated and do not provide evidence as to an Inspector’s fitness for or approach to a particular case
decision Makers handle different numbers of cases in a year – some dealing with as few as one which would give a result of 100% allowed or 100% dismissed
decision Makers are rigorously trained to ensure that they develop and maintain the skills necessary to undertake the work that they are given. These skills will influence the type of cases they deal with
some appeals are linked together as they relate to the same or similar development on the same site
the Inspectorate has an exacting Ministerial target which requires all casework to be 99% free from justified complaint or legal challenge
a Decision Maker constitutes a selected person appointed to carry out: open, impartial, honest decisions on behalf of the Secretary of State

1. Overview
1.1 This notice
This notice explains:
when building work can be zero-rated or reduced-rated at 5%
when building materials can be zero-rated or reduced-rated at 5%
when the sale, or long lease in a building is zero-rated
where you can find out more about the VAT domestic reverse charge for building and construction services
when developers are ‘blocked’ from deducting input tax on goods that are not building materials
when a builder or developer needs to have a certificate from their customer, confirming that the building concerned is intended to be used for a purpose that attracts the zero or reduced rate
when a customer can issue that certificate to a builder or developer
what happens when a certificated building is no longer used for the purpose that attracted the zero rate, the use for that purpose decreases or the building is disposed of
the special time of supply rules for builders
when a business, on using its own labour to carry out building work on a building or civil engineering structure that it occupies or uses, must account for a self-supply charge
1.2 Who should read this notice
You should read this notice if you:
are a contractor or subcontractor
are a developer
need to issue a certificate in order to obtain zero-rated or reduced-rated building work
need to issue a certificate in order to buy, or long lease, a zero-rated building
have issued the certificate and got zero rating but either no longer intend to use the building for a qualifying purpose, or dispose of the building
This notice may also help if you, as the customer or client of a contractor, subcontractor or developer, wish to satisfy yourself about the correct liability of the supplies of goods and services being made by them to you.
This is especially so in the case of DIY house builders and converters (‘self-builders’), who contract VAT-registered builders or tradesmen to carry out construction or conversion services and are charged VAT on those services.
Some, if not most, of the VAT charged can be recovered by the self-builder through the provisions of the DIY house builders and converters VAT refund scheme. However, only where that VAT refund scheme has been correctly charged in the first place.
You can read more about the VAT refund scheme in
Reclaim VAT on a self build home
.
1.3 The law
The Value Added Tax Act 1994, section 30 holds that goods and services specified in schedule 8 to the act are zero-rated.
Schedule 8, group 5 (as amended by Statutory Instruments 1995/280, 1997/50, 2001/2305, 2002/1101 and 2010/486) specifies when the construction (and the supply of building materials with those services), conversion of a non-residential building (and the supply of building materials with those services), sale, or long lease of a building is zero-rated.
Schedule 8, group 6 (as amended by Statutory Instruments 1995/283 and 1995/1625 (NI 9) and the Planning (Consequential Provisions) (Scotland) Act 1997) specifies when the alteration (and the supply of building materials with those services), sale, or long lease of a protected building is zero-rated.
The Value Added Tax Act 1994, section 29A (as inserted by the Finance Act 2001, section 99(4)) holds that goods and services specified in schedule 7A to the Act are reduced-rated.
Schedule 7A, group 6 (as inserted by Finance Act 2001, section 99(5) and amended by Statutory Instrument 2002/1100) specifies when a residential conversion is reduced-rated.
Schedule 7A, group 7 (as inserted by Finance Act 2001, section 99(5) and amended by Statutory Instruments 2002/1100 and 2007/3448) specifies when the renovation and alteration of a dwelling is reduced-rated.
Schedule 10, part 2 (as amended by Statutory Instruments 2002/1102 and 2011/86) specifies when a taxable self-supply arises, should the qualifying use of a certificated building cease or decrease or the building be disposed of.
The rules that ‘block’ developers from deducting input tax on goods that are not building materials are found in the VAT (Input Tax) Order 1992 (Statutory Instrument 1992/3222), articles 2 and 6 (as amended by Statutory Instrument 1995/281).
The special time of supply rules for builders are found in the Value Added Tax Regulations 1995 (Statutory Instrument 1995/2518), Regulations 89 and 93 (as amended by Statutory Instruments 1997/2887 and 1999/1374).
The rules for the self-supply of construction services are found in the Value Added Tax (Self-Supply of Construction Services) Order 1989 (Statutory Instrument 1989/472).
2. VAT liability
2.1 Construction services
The construction of a new building and work to an existing building is normally standard-rated. There are various exceptions to this.
Exceptions
The following are exceptions in the construction service:
