Book and plan your visit to Birmingham Prison
To visit someone in Birmingham prison you must:
be on that person’s visitor list
book your visit at least 2 days in advance
have the
required ID
with you when you go
If you have any questions about visiting you can contact the visitor centre by:
email
Birmingham@prisonadvice.org.uk
telephone 0121 598 8178 (Monday to Friday 10am to 3pm)
Help with the cost of your visit
If you get certain benefits or have an NHS health certificate, you might be able to
get help with the costs of your visit
, including:
travel to the prison
somewhere to stay overnight
meals
How to book family and friends visits
To arrange a visit, contact:
telephone 0333 207 2490
email
visits.birmingham@justice.gov.uk
The booking line opens, Monday to Friday 10am to 3pm
Find out about call charges
Visits take place every day of the week, including weekends.
Each prisoner can have up to 3 adults visitors and 3 children.
A maximum of £35 per table can be spent during a visit. Bank cards are accepted.
Visiting times
Monday to Sunday, 9:30am to 11:30am and 2pm to 4pm
How to book official visits
To arrange an official visit (legal only):
email
legalvisitsbirmingham@justice.gov.uk
Legal video visit times (1 hour slots) :
Monday to Friday, 9am, 10am, 11am, 2pm, 3pm and 4pm
We recommend legal video appointments as the wait times are significantly less.
Legal face to face appointments are available (1 hour slots):
Monday, Wednesday and Thursday only, 9am, 10am, 11am, 2pm, 3pm and 4pm
To arrange an official appointment (non-legal)
All other official video appointments (non-legal) please email
VCCBirmingham@justice.gov.uk
Official (non-legal) video appointment times (1 hour slots)
Monday to Friday, 8.30am to 5pm
Important information for all official appointments:
requests for appointments longer than 1 hour will only be considered in exceptional circumstances. You must include full justification when you email. Agreement will be subject to operational availability and management approval.
All official appointment requests must be submitted via CJSM or an official work email account.
You must present valid photographic ID at the start of all video and in-person visits, or your appointment may be cancelled.
Before attending a face to face appointment, please read the
entering Birmingham section
.
Visitors must be named on the booking 24 hours before the appointment date to gain entry.
If you have any issues on the day of your video appointment, you can contact
VCCBirmingham@justice.gov.uk
or contact 0121 598 8252.
Getting to Birmingham Prison
Find Birmingham Prison on a map
Birmingham Prison is about 2 miles from Birmingham New Street Station, where you can take a taxi or change onto local buses and trams. The closest tram station is Winson Green Outer Circle.
To plan your journey by public transport:
use
National Rail enquiries
use
Network West Midlands for transport in Birmingham
There is a free visitors car park with disability access.
Entering Birmingham Prison
All visitors, aged 16 or older must prove their identity before entering the prison.
Read the list of acceptable forms of ID for all visitors.
.
All visitors will need to be given a pat-down search, including children. You may also be sniffed by security dogs.
You will be told the rules by an officer at the start of your visit. If you break the rules, your visit could be cancelled and you could be banned from visiting again.
Dress code
We ask all visitors to dress appropriately when attending the prison. This helps ensure visits can take place safely, respectfully, and without disruption.
The following items are not permitted:
coats, long cardigans, or other outerwear
hats (except for religious headwear), gloves, scarves, shawls or ties
knee-high or knee-length boots
shorts (of any length)
ripped or distressed trousers or jeans
combat-style trousers with external pockets
figure-hugging jumpsuits
clothing that may reveal underwear or draw attention to intimate areas
clothing with offensive or inappropriate logos or patterns (for example cannabis-related, racist or offensive language)
sports clothing, including football shirts or visible sports logos
hooded tops or tops with pockets
Skirts and dresses must be at least calf length when seated (even if worn with tights or leggings).
Tops and dresses must fully cover the chest, including the cleavage and midriff.
All headwear will be searched in line with HMP Birmingham’s searching procedures.
There are strict controls on what you can take into the prison. You will have to leave most of the things you have with you in a locker or with security. Pushchairs and car seats can be brought as far as the visitor waiting area.
Pushchairs are allowed upstairs but must be left outside the visits hall in the visitors waiting area. 1 basic car seat/ carry cot can be brought into the room which must remain on the floor.
Call the booking line if you have any questions about visiting 01215 988 178.
Visiting facilities
There will be refreshments available during your visit and a children’s play area is available to use.
Family days
There are 6 family days per year. For more information, please contact 01215 988 178.
Keep in touch with someone at Birmingham Prison
There are several ways you can keep in touch with someone during their time at Birmingham Prison.
Secure video calls
To have a secure video call with someone in this prison you need to:
Download the
Prison Video app
Create an account
Register all visitors
Add the prisoner to your contact list
How to book a secure video call
Secure video calls at this prison can be requested by prisoners only.
You will receive a notification if a prisoner has requested a video call with you.
Read more about how Prison Video works
Phone calls
Prisoners have phones in their cells and are able to make calls every day between 7am and 11pm.
Phones do not accept incoming calls so they will always have to call you. They have to buy phone credits to do this.
They can phone anyone named on their list of friends and family. This list is checked by security when they first arrive so it may take a few days before they are able to call.
You can also exchange voicemails using the
Prison Voicemail service
.
Officers may listen to phone calls as a way of preventing crime and helping keep people safe.
Email
You can send emails to someone in Birmingham Prison using the
Email a Prisoner service
.
You might also be able to attach photos and receive replies, depending on the rules at Birmingham Prison.
Letters
You can write at any time.
Include the prisoners name and prison number on the envelope.
If you do not know their prison number,
contact Birmingham Prison
.
All post apart from legal letters will be opened and checked by officers.
Send money and gifts
You can use the free and fast
online service to send money to someone in prison
.
You can no longer send money by bank transfer, cheque, postal order or send cash by post.
If you cannot use the online service, you may be able to
apply for an exemption
- for example if you:
are unable to use a computer, a smart phone or the internet
do not have a debit card
This will allow you to send money by post.
Gifts and parcels
Prisoners in Birmingham Prison have a list of approved items that can be given to them by family and friends.
Prisoners must first apply for permission to receive items. Birmingham Prison then sends the family member or friend an approved stamp to fix to their parcel.
Family and friends can then hand in the parcel before visits.
Items should be handed in to the property desk in the visitors centre.
You must have a visit booked for the time you hand anything in, otherwise it won’t be accepted.
Items are not normally accepted by post. However, a prisoner who is a foreign national or does not get visits can apply for permission for a family member or friend to send items in. These parcels must also be marked with an approved stamp. Birmingham Prison takes no responsibility for items sent in the post.
Make sure to include the prisoner’s name and prison number on parcels. All items will be opened and inspected by an officer.
Friends and families of prisoners are permitted to send books directly to their loved ones, or can order books from approved retailers, which can source and send the books on to prisoners.
For the full list of approved retailers, you can read
Prison education and library services, Annex A
.
Contact Birmingham Prison
if you have any questions.
Life at Birmingham Prison
Birmingham Prison is committed to providing a safe and educational environment where prisoners can learn new skills to help them on release.
Security and safeguarding
Every prisoner at Birmingham Prison has a right to feel safe. The staff are responsible for their safeguarding and welfare at all times.
For further information about what to do when you are worried or concerned about someone in prison
visit the Prisoners’ Families helpline website
.
Arrival and first night
When someone first arrives at Birmingham Prison, they will be able to contact a family member by phone. This could be quite late in the evening, depending on the time they arrive.
They will get to speak to someone who will check how they’re feeling and ask about any immediate health and wellbeing needs.
Induction
Each prisoner who arrives at Birmingham Prison gets an induction that lasts about 3 days. They will meet professionals who will help them with:
health and wellbeing, including mental and sexual health
any substance misuse issues, including drugs and alcohol
personal development in custody and on release, including skills, education and training
other support (sometimes called ‘interventions’), such as managing difficult emotions
Everyone also finds out about the rules, fire safety, and how things like calls and visits work.
Accommodation
Around 1,000 prisoners are at Birmingham Prison in a mixture of single and shared cells. There are 11 wings, including an older prisoners unit, a drug recovery unit and a first night centre.
Facilities include a library and gym.
Birmingham Prison has a diverse, multi-faith chaplaincy team providing support to prisoners.
Education and work
Prisoners have access to a broad range of vocational training, including bricklaying, plumbing, painting and decorating, carpentry, forklift truck driving, industrial cleaning and catering.
They can also take courses in basic skills, IT, social and life skills, business skills, creative and performing arts, barbering and more. Students have the opportunity to gain recognised qualifications on all courses. The education is provided by Novus.
Birmingham Prison has an active resettlement unit which helps prisoners with housing, benefits and employment issues supported by staff from Job Centre Plus and Citizens Advice.
Temporary release
Some prisoners may qualify for release on temporary licence. This can be used to gain work experience in the local community and prepare for release. Prisoners can apply for this within the prison.
Support for family and friends
At HMP Birmingham we understand how important it is that our prisoners receive support from their families and loved ones.
You can read the Birmingham family strategy
to see how we help prisoners build positive relationships with loved ones.
You can also find out about
advice and helplines for family and friends
.
Family services at Birmingham are provided by
PACT
.
Information on services and support for families and friends is also available from the visitors centre.
Concerns, problems and complaints
In an emergency
Call 0121 598 8000  if you think a prisoner is at immediate risk of harm. Ask for the Orderly Officer and explain that your concern is an emergency.

0800 917 6877

This number can be called anonymously. If you are concerned about a prisoner being bullied by a member of staff, you can use this number. As this line is managed separately from the prison, you can call this number anonymously.

.

Press release
HM Land Registry to provide property identifiers for Price Paid Data from 28 August
Unique Property Reference Numbers (UPRNs) and INSPIRE IDs will be included with the monthly Price Paid Data dataset, making it easier to match and analyse property data.
From:
HM Land Registry
Published:
26 August 2026
Richard Whitcombe/Shutterstock.com
Unique Property Reference Numbers (UPRNs) and
INSPIRE IDs
are to be made available alongside the monthly Price Paid Data dataset from 28 August 2026
Used alongside other location-based services, these trusted property identifiers will support more accurate matching and analysis
The enhancement responds to customer demand and helps unlock greater value from land and property data
From 28 August 2026, HM Land Registry will provide Unique Property Reference Numbers (UPRNs) and INSPIRE IDs in separate lookup tables alongside the monthly Price Paid dataset.
This responds to customer demand for UPRNs and INSPIRE IDs to be included alongside Price Paid Data, making it easier to connect sale price information with other property and location datasets.
Price Paid Data includes information about residential property sales in England and Wales. It is used by property professionals, researchers, public bodies, lenders, digital service providers and others who need reliable property market information.
Benefits
The lookup tables will make it easier to link Price Paid Data with other data sources, supporting its use alongside mapping tools and location-based services.
Introducing these trusted property and spatial identifiers will support more accurate matching and enable better analysis, reporting and digital services.
Providing UPRNs and INSPIRE IDs supports wider government objectives and HM Land Registry’s ambition to unlock greater value from land and property data through improved connectivity, interoperability and reuse.
External data providers and organisations will  benefit  from more reliable, comprehensive, and linked datasets, enabling innovation in property data services, analytics, and digital products.
Lynne Nicholson, Deputy Director for Data at HM Land Registry, said:
We have a strategic plan to unlock the value of our data to create new opportunities for innovation and growth. To support this, and in response to customer demand, we are providing UPRNs and INSPIRE IDs through a series of lookup tables, beginning with our Price Paid dataset. Later this financial year, we will be adding similar lookup tables to our UK Companies data and Overseas Companies data, as part of our move to support a more efficient, transparent, and digitally connected property market.
GeoPlace manages the official national address and street databases for England and Wales including the allocation of a range of UPRNs to local authorities and Ordnance Survey.
Nick Chapallaz, Managing Director at GeoPlace, said:
HM Land Registry has already established a valuable link between title numbers and UPRNs, helping connect property ownership information with authoritative location data. Extending that approach to Price Paid Data is a natural next step. As a persistent, unique identifier maintained through local authority address custodians and GeoPlace, the UPRN provides certainty of reference across the property sector, ensuring that different organisations are working with the same property, regardless of how its address appears in their systems. That shared reference point enables property data from different sources to be linked, analysed and mapped, opening up new opportunities for insight across the property market.
Potential uses of the UPRNs and INSPIRE IDs alongside the Price Paid Data dataset
Estate agents and property portals
More accurate listing data: Linking Price Paid Data to UPRNs would help agents and portals match historic sale prices to the correct property, reducing errors caused by inconsistent addresses or duplicate records.
Clearer property history: A stable property identifier would make it easier to show a reliable transaction history for a specific property, improving transparency for buyers and sellers.
Financial institutions and lenders
More reliable property matching: UPRNs would give lenders a consistent way to connect sale price, address and property records, reducing uncertainty during valuation, mortgage assessment and due diligence.
Improved risk analysis: INSPIRE IDs would help link transaction values to land parcels and spatial data, supporting clearer assessment of location-based risks and property context.
Developers and investors
Better site and land analysis: INSPIRE IDs would allow developers and investors to connect sold-price information to land parcels and boundaries, supporting more accurate site assembly and opportunity assessment.
More granular market insight: Linking prices to UPRNs and INSPIRE IDs would enable analysis at property, street, neighbourhood and land-parcel level, supporting better investment and planning decisions.
Government and researchers
Stronger policy insight: Linking Price Paid Data with UPRNs and INSPIRE IDs would help government and researchers analyse housing markets more accurately across properties, places and land parcels.
Better data integration: Stable identifiers would make it easier to connect price information with other public datasets, reducing matching errors and improving the evidence base for local and national decisions.
Homebuyers and sellers
Reduced confusion: UPRNs and INSPIRE IDs would help reduce issues caused by address changes, similar property names or inconsistent address formats, supporting smoother property transactions.
Background
A UPRN is a unique number which identifies an addressable location.
INSPIRE stands for Infrastructure for Spatial Information in Europe. It is a European Union initiative and legal framework established in May 2007 to create a standardised spatial data infrastructure. An INSPIRE ID is an automatically generated unique number given to a specific shape on a map (polygon) that outlines a piece of land or property. This links the spatial data to official land registry records, helping people match map locations with legal ownership data.
Local authorities are responsible for creating new addresses and assigning each property a UPRN. They send updates to
GeoPlace
, which adds them to the national databases. The information is then shared with Ordnance Survey and included in its address products and mapping services.
Price Paid Data
is property price data for all residential and commercial property sales in England and Wales that are lodged with HM Land Registry for registration in that month,
subject to exclusions
.
Price Paid Data
is published at 11am on the 20th working day of each month.
The lookup tables will apply to monthly Price Paid Data published from 28 August 2026 onwards and will not be available for previously published datasets.
The lookup table for the current monthly Price Paid Data dataset will be available from 28 August through HM Land Registry’s existing public data channels.
Customers will be able to download the identifiers and use them with their existing data matching, analysis and reporting processes.
Price Paid Data can be downloaded in text, CSV format and in a machine readable format as
linked data
and is released under
Open Government Licence (OGL)
. Under the OGL, HM Land Registry permits the use of Price Paid Data for commercial or non-commercial purposes. However, the OGL does not cover the use of
third party rights
, which HM Land Registry is not authorised to license.
HM Land Registry safeguards land and property ownership worth nearly £9 trillion across England and Wales, playing a vital role in supporting the property market, home buying and the Governments ambitions for housing and economic growth.
Find further information about
HM Land Registry
.
HM Land Registry’s
Strategy 2025+
affirms its commitment to continue working with others across the sector to build a simpler, faster and more transparent property market.

Press release
Consumer upgrades for two housing associations
The Regulator of Social Housing has published regulatory judgements for four housing associations including two consumer upgrades.
From:
Regulator of Social Housing
Published:
26 August 2026
Two housing associations received C1 consumer upgrades in regulatory judgements published by the Regulator of Social Housing today.
Livin Housing Limited and Community Gateway Association Limited were both upgraded from C2 to C1
RSH
found that Livin, which is based in County Durham, had strengthened its understanding of the condition of its homes since its inspection in November 2024.
The housing association has improved how it monitors the condition of its homes and uses that information to plan future repairs and investment. Livin also demonstrated that it works more effectively with residents to maintain safe, good quality homes.
Community Gateway, based in Preston, Lancashire, demonstrated it had strengthened its health and safety management since its inspection in July 2025.
It had also improved governance and accountability, demonstrating that its repairs and maintenance services are working well. It was also communicating better with tenants and had increased understanding of their diverse needs.
Kate Dodsworth, Deputy Chief Executive at
RSH
, said: “Landlords that achieve a C1 grading show they are putting tenants at the heart of their services, maintaining safe and decent homes, and responding effectively when issues arise.
“We expect landlords to use good quality information and strong governance to drive improvements, support thriving communities, and help meet housing need through the delivery of more and better social homes.”
Both Livin and Community Gateway have unchanged G1 governance and V1 financial viability grades based on previous assessments.
Amplius Living has received gradings of C2, G1 and V2 today, following inspection. The housing association, based in Milton Keynes was formed following the merger of Longhurst Group Limited and Grand Union Housing Group Limited in December 2024.
Amplius showed
RSH
it has appropriate systems in place to ensure the health and safety of its tenants and a good understanding of compliance requirements.
However, there was evidence of weaknesses in the provision of an effective, efficient and timely repairs service, with complaints and customer feedback showing issues around service quality and communication. Amplius also experienced challenges in meeting the increased legal requirements for tackling damp and mould following the introduction of Awaab’s Law.
Amplius is addressing the issues, but
RSH
said it would need to evidence continued and consistent improvement to demonstrate the required outcomes for tenants on an ongoing basis.
Hertfordshire-based Watford Community Housing Trust received an interim judgement today, confirming a G1 governance grade and a V2 financial viability grade.
RSH
issued the interim judgement because Watford Community Housing (trading as Chime Housing) merged with Thrive Homes in June 2026.
RSH
has not yet assessed the merged entity against the consumer standards.

Press release
Grenfell Tower Crown development application given approval
The Grenfell Tower Crown development application has today been given approval by the Planning Inspectorate.
From:
Planning Inspectorate
Published:
25 August 2026
The application was submitted to the Planning Inspectorate by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government and accepted for examination on 27 May 2026.
The development involves works to take down Grenfell Tower to ground level from its original height of 24 storeys, which commenced in September 2025 under permitted development rights.
The decision to approve was made following a written representations procedure, during which the public, statutory consultees and interested parties were given the opportunity to make representations on the application.
The decision notice including a statement setting out the reasons for the decision can be found on the
Crown Development Applications project page
.
Notes to editors
The government has implemented two new routes by which Crown bodies can apply for planning permission for development on Crown land in England.
One Crown Development route allows planning applications for Crown developments which are considered of ‘national importance’ to be submitted to the Planning Inspectorate directly instead of to local planning authorities.
Applications taken through this route are determined on the basis of their planning merits, with due consideration of local and national planning policy. Comprehensive engagement takes place with local communities and local planning authorities throughout the decision-making process.
This process is led by an independent Planning Inspector, or a panel of planning Inspectors, appointed by the Secretary of State.
Crown land is defined in
section 293 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990
as land in which there is a Crown interest or a Duchy interest.
‘Crown interest’ is defined as an interest belonging to His Majesty in right of the Crown or in right of his private estates, an interest belonging to a government department or held in trust for His Majesty for the purposes of a government department, and such other interest as the Secretary of State specifies by order.
‘Duchy interest’ is defined as an interest belonging to His Majesty in right of the Duchy of Lancaster or belonging to the Duchy of Cornwall.
Note: Applications for Crown Developments which are considered of ‘national importance’ and time sensitive and critical to national interests will be made directly to the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government MHCLG.

Capacity to Build (2026 to 2029)
The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (
MHCLG
) is investing a further £46 million over 3 years to expand its skills and capacity offer to councils in a re-branded programme – Capacity to Build. Following the success of the £17 million invested in skills and capacity since 2025, Capacity to Build will continue to help councils develop ambitious pipelines, overcome barriers to delivery and strengthen specialist housing capacity.
Capacity to Build is delivered in partnership with Homes England and the Local Government Association (
LGA
) and will run between April 2026 and March 2029, helping councils to:
improve their workforce‘s capability to deliver social and affordable housing
recruit and retain staff to specialist housebuilding positions
develop and accelerate bids for grant funding through the Social and Affordable Homes Programme (
SAHP
)
Capacity to Build can support councils of all abilities, including those who may not have built any new social and affordable housing for some time. The programme has 3 complementary elements:
the Council Housebuilding Support Service
the Council Housebuilding Support Fund
the Pathways to Planning graduate scheme
The Council Housebuilding Support Service
The Council Housebuilding Support Service (
CHoSS
) is delivered by the
LGA
and aims to provide up to 225 tailored support packages between April 2026 and March 2029. Councils may receive more than one package of support where different or additional needs are identified.
Following an assessment of each council’s housing delivery capability and support needs,
CHoSS
provides bespoke no-cost support to help councils establish, strengthen, or accelerate their council housebuilding programmes. Support may include technical and specialist advice, training, workshops, tools, published guidance, and peer learning.
Further information about
CHoSS
, including how councils can register their interest or request a conversation with a Senior Regional Adviser, is available on the
CHoSS
page of the
LGA
’s website
.
For clarity, councils receiving support through
CHoSS
can also access the Council Housebuilding Support Fund, but only to address a separate issue or challenge.
An expansion of the Pathways to Planning programme
Capacity to Build includes an expanded Pathways to Planning offer. Already delivered by the
LGA
to bring in talent to planning teams, this expanded programme allows councils to recruit and retain recent graduates to other specialist housebuilding positions, including surveying and construction project management roles.
Graduates are supported through structured training and accreditation routes, helping councils to build a sustainable pipeline of skilled staff for housing delivery.
These 2 new pathways aim to recruit up to 150 graduates during 2026 to 2029. Onboarding will commence from early 2027.
Further information about the expanded Pathways to Planning programme is available on the
Pathways to Planning page of the
LGA
’s website
.
The Council Housebuilding Support Fund
The Council Housebuilding Support Fund (
CHSF
) is delivered in partnership with Homes England and provides councils with targeted revenue funding to support early stage housing development activity.
In 2025 to 2026,
CHSF
provided grant funding to 44 councils, helping to develop and accelerate bids to the
SAHP
leading to approximately 11,500 homes.
Over the next 3 years,
CHSF
will continue to help councils to fund pre development work, including:
feasibility and viability studies
site investigations and technical due diligence
pipeline development and preparation
All grant funding awarded through
CHSF
is for the express purpose of helping councils to bring forward large and ambitious bids to
SAHP
.
Further information about
CHSF
, including eligibility and eligible activity, is available on the
CHSF
page on GOV.UK
.
Details of how councils can apply for funding through the 2026 to 2027 bidding round will be published in September 2026.

Scope and purpose of the fund
The Council Housebuilding Support Fund aims to help councils:
increase delivery of new-build, affordable homes, through the
Social and Affordable Homes Programme
(
SAHP
)
maximise the number of homes available for social rent
ensure regional and place-based affordable housing priorities are delivered (in an Established Mayoral Strategic Authority (
EMSA
) area) wherever possible
What your proposal could include
We are looking for applicants to demonstrate and evidence how their proposal contributes to these aims and supports delivery of new social and affordable homes through the Social and Affordable Homes Programme.
If you received funding from 1 or both of the following schemes, we will expect you to evidence how you have completed activities for which you received funding. These schemes are:
an earlier round of the Council Housebuilding Support Fund (
CHSF
)
the
Council Housebuilding Support Service
(
CHoSS
)
We will also ask you to confirm that, should you receive further funding, it will not be used to deliver the same activities and evidence how this funding will unlock additional affordable housing delivery.
We offer the following guidance on what we are looking for in relation to these aims:
Submitting a subsequent bid for grant funding to the Social and Affordable Homes Programme
You must show how your proposal will support you to submit a bid to the Social and Affordable Homes Programme and, or, bring forward a planned bid more quickly than would otherwise be the case.
You should show how your proposal will increase the number of new affordable homes you will be able to deliver, compared to your existing plans.
Plans where activities are intended to unlock estate regeneration opportunities will be considered if there is a clear commitment and plan to increase the supply of new council housing.
We are keen to support plans for councils to deliver new affordable homes directly or in partnerships with other registered providers or developers. Ideally, these partnerships should result in council ownership of the homes, but we will also consider applications where the homes are owned by another registered provider.
Maximising the number of social rent homes delivered
We are looking for you to demonstrate how your proposal will lead to the delivery of homes for Social Rent.
Plans to deliver mixed-tenure schemes are acceptable where they can evidence local housing need.
Delivering regional and place-based housing priorities
Established Mayoral Strategic Authorities (
EMSAs
) are able to set the strategic direction of the Social and Affordable Homes Programme in their area, including shaping the tenure and mix of a scheme and identifying priority sites.
We are looking for councils in these areas to demonstrate how their proposal will help them deliver their
EMSA
’s affordable housing priorities
.
Assessment criteria
When making an application, councils are encouraged to show a clear link between proposed activities and their ability to create ambitious and high-quality bids to the Social and Affordable Homes Programme.
Applications will be assessed to ensure the funding can deliver maximum impact.
The following criteria will be used:
value for money
deliverability
strategic fit
Value for money
Proposals will be assessed on the basis of value for money to ensure the funding can deliver maximum impact.
To ensure the funding supports as many councils as possible, councils will be expected to maximise the use of their own funding to deliver their proposals.
Proposals need to show:
total costs
the amount of funding requested
milestones and delivery timescales for spend associated with your proposals
confirmation of the councils’ own funding and resources used to deliver activities and projects in addition to this funding
Deliverability
Funding is expected to be spent in the financial year in which it is awarded. You will need to demonstrate how activities and expenditure can be delivered within this timeframe. Early spend and delivery will be prioritised.
Additional weighting will be given to proposals that will support councils to submit bids to the Social and Affordable Homes Programme early and deliver additional affordable homes before mid-2029.
Proposals need to show:
a clear plan and milestones to deliver the activities described including start and completion dates for the social and affordable homes to be delivered as a result
the councils’ capability and capacity to undertake the activities described (including any recent, relevant track record of delivery)
how and when the activities described will allow a bid for grant funding to the Social and Affordable Homes Programme
any risks to delivery and planned mitigations
Strategic fit
Proposals will be assessed to take account of the extent to which they deliver 1 or more of the aims of the funding. These aims are described elsewhere in the guidance.
There will be a particular focus on proposals that will enable councils to meet the strategic objectives of the Social and Affordable Homes Programme.
Proposals must show evidence of how activities will support the council to:
increase the speed and scale at which they could bid for grant funding via the Social and Affordable Homes Programme, compared to existing plans
plan for and meet the wider aims of the Social and Affordable Homes Programme
The proposals must clearly show the types of new affordable homes the activities are intended to support the planning for and delivery of.

) more quickly and at a bigger scale than would otherwise be possible.
It supports councils to:
deliver more new affordable homes (directly or in partnership with registered providers or developers)
develop plans that maximise the number of homes delivered for social rent
ensure regional and place-based affordable housing priorities are delivered (in an Established Mayoral Strategic Authority (
EMSA
) area) wherever possible
Applications should show how proposals will strengthen the council’s ability to be able to bring forward bids for the
Social and Affordable Homes Programme
(
SAHP
)  including by increasing the scale, quality or pace of future delivery.
Applications could include proposals for activities or projects including:
knowledge development — such as training and upskilling staff, improving knowledge and understanding of process and bidding for the Social and Affordable Homes Programme
pipeline development — such as commissioning studies to identify a long list of deliverable sites or developing delivery strategies to unlock identified sites
pre-development and enabling work — such as technical expertise and support to bring forward sites and secure planning permission
partnership working — such as supporting engagement, co-ordination and joint working opportunities with registered providers and developers
additional staffing — such as interim staff, project managers, and consultants that bring relevant technical expertise
What cannot be funded
The fund cannot support applications for funding where proposals include:
costs that have already been incurred
activities that have already taken place
costs that can be capitalised to the project that they relate
costs that can be funded through other means (such as proposals where council resources have already been allocated)
funding that would cover day-to-day expenditure (applications to cover staff or consultants must show how the work they will be doing relates to new activity)
business-as-usual costs such as activity that would have already taken place
Who should apply
Funding from the Council Housebuilding Support Fund is available to all councils in England (outside of London).
We particularly encourage applications from:
councils already delivering through the Social and Affordable Homes Programme who, with additional support, could increase the number of new affordable homes delivered
councils close to delivering through the Social and Affordable Homes Programme and with additional support could submit ambitious new proposals
councils exploring partnerships with private registered providers and developers, who, with additional support, could speed up or increase delivery
Available funding
£21.8 million in funding is available until 31 March 2029, split evenly across each of the 3 financial years.
Councils can submit a single proposal up to a maximum of £300,000 in each of the 3 years. A proposal can cover multiple activities.
How to apply
Your application should evidence how your proposal aligns with the overall objectives of the fund. It should show a clear link between proposed activities and your ability to create ambitious and high-quality bids to the Social and Affordable Homes Programme.
Find out about
assessment criteria for the Council Housebuilding Support Fund
. Strong applications will clearly demonstrate value for money, deliverability and strategic fit with the objectives of the fund.
Applications will open in September 2026 for funding that will start to be used from financial year 2026 and 2027.
You will be able to apply online when the bidding window opens.
Future bidding windows are expected to open in April 2027 and April 2028 and information will be provided.
Data you provide is used to administer the fund and is subject to both the:
Capacity to Build privacy notice
Homes England privacy notice
After you’ve applied
Applications will be assessed as they are submitted.
Find out about the
assessment criteria for the Council Housebuilding Support Fund
.
We will contact you using the contact details provided when you submit your bid. You will hear whether you have been successful or not from November 2026.
If your bid is successful
Successful applicants will be expected to enter into a memorandum of understanding with
MHCLG
, setting out the activities, milestones and reporting requirements associated with the funding.
Funding is expected to be spent in the financial year in which it is awarded. Further information on expenditure profiles, reporting requirements and any arrangements relating to extensions will be set out in the memorandum of understanding.
Monitoring arrangements will be put in place and an evaluation undertaken at the end of the fund. Councils will be required to provide monitoring information on funded activities. Councils may also be asked to contribute to programme evaluation activity.
Read
if your bid to the Council Housebuilding Support Fund is successful
to find out more.
How to get help

have questions about the fund

email

.
You can also discuss proposals before applying with your regular contact in Homes England’s Regional Affordable Housing Growth team. If you do not have a regular contact in the team email

.

Press release
Every care leaver to have someone in their corner after review
£25 million investment to help thousands more care leavers access homes with support and connection.
From:
Department for Education
and
Josh MacAlister OBE MP
Published:
25 August 2026
Thousands more young people leaving care will have people around them when they move into adulthood, as the government begins the national rollout of a strengthened housing programme backed by £25 million this year alone. The programme will grow high quality and innovative housing models that build connection around those leaving care.
It comes as a government-commissioned independent review into the early deaths of young people who left care is published today, led by author and broadcaster Ashley John-Baptiste and social work leader Clare Chamberlain.
The review tells the stories of six young people who died between the ages of 18 and 24. Those who knew them describe them as devoted, bubbly, kind, and deeply loved. They were also, in the words of one young person quoted in the report, ‘on their own’.
Its central finding is that young people leaving care are profoundly isolated. Services often respond to a young person’s understandable wish for their own place, but independence can arrive with an unexpected loneliness and no one close enough to notice when things go wrong.
The report sets out three things that must change: how young people are prepared for adulthood, the sharp drop in help at age 18, and the skills of the workforce supporting them.
In response, government is driving forward the national rollout of connected housing options for those leaving care, starting with £25 million this year alone. This marks a major change that will make the Staying Close programme focused on expanding housing models akin to Shared Lives Plus, The House Project and Supported Lodgings to every part of the country. For young people, this will significantly increase their chances of being offered a home that provides them with community and connection rather than leaving them isolated in inappropriate accommodation.
Children’s Minister Josh MacAlister said:
Every one of these young lives mattered, and behind each of them lies a story of enormous loss – for their families, for their friends, and for the people who cared for them.
We owe it to these young people, and to every care experienced person, to change care so that we make enduring relationships the central obsession of the care system. Care must build and not break the relationships that young people need, and this must be the new north star.
I am incredibly grateful to Ashley and Clare for their work on this review. The tragic stories they have captured must galvanise us to make sure that no one leaving care is left isolated and alone. This will be a whole society effort, so I urge everyone to play their part.
Author and broadcaster Ashley John-Baptise said:
As a care experienced broadcaster, I’ve been privileged to cover many aspects of the care system. That said, nothing could have prepared me for the devastating stories we’ve come across whilst doing this work.
The lives of these care leavers mattered. I really hope our review shines a light on who they were, how they were failed and serves as a useful report to stir us all.
Social work leader, Clare Chamberlain said:
This review has reinforced what care leavers have told us for years: the state is no substitute for family. 
We need to do more to prevent the acute loneliness that the most vulnerable experience after leaving care
In 2025, 112 deaths of care leavers aged 18 to 24 were notified to the Department for Education. That is an estimated 130 per 100,000, around three to four times the rate for others the same age. Ashley and Clare were commissioned to undertake this review by the Children’s Minister after he identified repeated patterns in the reports of these early deaths.
Through the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Act, more public bodies will become corporate parents, meaning the NHS, jobcentres, prisons, and probation must weigh what care leavers need when they design services. New duties from 30 September require councils to publish how they will support care leavers into independent living, and from that date a care leaver can no longer be found intentionally homeless.

Press release
Historic council housebuilding comeback to help families into secure homes
The government announces its first wave of funding from its £39bn Social and Affordable Homes Programme.
From:
Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
,
The Rt Hon Andy Burnham MP
and
The Rt Hon Angela Rayner MP
Published:
24 August 2026
Families stuck without a secure home to benefit from the first wave of funding from the government’s £39bn Social and Affordable Homes Programme
Councils backed to build more homes as ministers drive the biggest council housebuilding revival in decades
More decisions over housing investment to move closer to local communities
Families trapped in temporary accommodation or stuck on housing waiting lists will be helped into safe, secure homes as the government kickstarts its record £39bn Social and Affordable Homes Programme.
Today (25 August) the Prime Minister and Secretary of State, Angela Rayner, are announcing nearly £10 billion of allocations to build thousands more quality council, social and affordable homes.
The first wave of funding announced today will support the delivery of more than 70,000 homes across England. It will go to 33 Strategic Partners – councils, housing associations and other providers that have secured long-term funding certainty to deliver homes at scale. Today’s announcement also marks a major step in the ambition to getting councils building at scale again.
Alongside housing associations, councils will be awarded Strategic Partner status with Homes England, helping put them firmly back at the heart of housebuilding. Around 60% of homes delivered through these partnerships are expected to be for Social Rent, the most affordable form of rented housing, helping more families access a secure home.
With almost 180,000 children growing up without a permanent home, the government is putting councils at the heart of housebuilding.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said:
No child should be raised in a hostel room and no family should wait ten years for a front door of their own. I have said from my first day in this job that everything starts with a good home.
Nearly £10 billion will go to councils and housing associations to build genuinely affordable homes, most of them for social rent, in the places where families are waiting longest.
Councils built this country out of a housing crisis once before. Backed properly, and trusted to get on with it, they will do it again.
Secretary of State Angela Rayner said:
Families can’t be left raising children without a place to call home, and none of us should spend years waiting for somewhere safe and affordable to live.
I know how important fixing this is – because I’ve been there. A safe and secure home was the foundation for a better life - I couldn’t have got to where I have today without it.
That’s why the Prime Minister and I are doing everything we can to get councils building once again – it’s fundamental to turning the housing crisis around, helping families out of temporary accommodation and into a secure home.
Over £2 billion of today’s funding is expected to be spent in Mayoral areas outside of London. As part of the government’s wider devolution agenda, Established Mayoral Strategic Authorities are setting the strategic direction for the programme in their areas, helping ensure investment reflects local priorities.
Over time, more funding is expected to flow directly to mayoral authorities as the programme develops, building on the Government’s commitment to move power and decision-making out of Whitehall.
Today’s allocation is only the first stage of the ten-year programme. More than £16 billion remains to be allocated outside London and in allocating this funding, we intend to prioritise Social Rent homes and council housebuilding, helping deliver the largest expansion of council housing in decades.
Amy Rees, Chief Executive Officer at Homes England said:
Today’s announcement marks an important step in delivering the government’s £39 billion Social and Affordable Homes Programme. Through these strategic partnerships and continuous market engagement, alongside Homes England’s wider investment including through the National Housing Bank, we can help unlock thousands of much-needed homes across England. By working with councils, mayors, housing associations and local partners, we can support the return of council housebuilding at scale, increase the supply of social rent homes and create thriving places that people are proud to call home.
Today’s package goes further by helping councils access more of the funding available to the programme and make full use of Right to Buy receipts – with £1.61 billion raised from sales alone in the last financial year – and other available funding streams.
To support this ambition, the government is investing a further £46 million over the next three years to strengthen councils’ skills, expertise and capacity to bring forward ambitious housebuilding plans.
London will receive a major boost for housebuilding, reflecting the acute need for affordable housing in the capital.
The Greater London Authority intends to offer at least £6 billion through the programme, with councils expected to deliver more than half of the homes funded in London. The capital is already demonstrating what can be achieved when local leaders have greater control over housing investment and delivery.
The Mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, said:
Tackling the housing crisis is one of my top priorities and I’m doing everything I can to deliver more affordable homes that Londoners desperately need. We’ve built record numbers of council homes in London, but the number of families and children without a permanent home stuck on housing waiting lists is still unacceptable. I want to work with this new Government to deliver a step change in how many council homes we can deliver across the capital.
Thousands of Londoners will benefit from this new wave of new social and affordable homes, which will help people out of temporary accommodation and provide good, affordable homes to live in for the long-term, as we build a fairer, better London for everyone.
Housing associations and other providers will continue to play a vital role in delivering the social and affordable homes the country needs.
Alongside councils, they will be central to delivering the Government’s ambition to increase housebuilding and expand access to genuinely affordable homes.
Kate Henderson, Chief Executive of the National Housing Federation, said:
It is hugely welcome to see this much-anticipated funding confirmed, something we have been calling for to kickstart construction on tens of thousands of desperately needed new social homes.
This is a major vote of confidence in not-for-profit housing associations and in the vital and distinct role they play in this country, as organisations that work for the long-term benefit of their communities.
Housing associations have risen to the challenge of delivering the governments ambitions. Working in partnership with government, councils and mayors, they have used the support and certainty provided by government to rebuild their development capacity, invest in skills, and be the strong and reliable partners needed to build a new generation of social and affordable homes, alongside increasing investment in their existing homes. This is no better demonstrated than in the scale and ambition of the bids submitted to this Social and Affordable Homes Programme.
We will continue work with national and local government to maximise housing associations’ potential to deliver new social rented homes during this parliament and over the next decade, meeting the housing needs of local people in every part of the country.
The package builds on the government’s commitment to deliver 1.5 million homes this Parliament, including the biggest boost to council, social and affordable housing in a generation.
Gavin Smart, Chief Executive at the Chartered Institute of Housing, said:
It’s very welcome to see funding from last year’s Spending Review now being allocated and getting into the hands of Strategic Partners across the country, turning the government’s long-term commitment into homes that can make a real difference for families. We welcome the strong focus on homes for social rent and the ambition for council housebuilding, and the recognition of the vital role that councils, housing associations and other providers will play in delivering the next generation of genuinely affordable homes. If delivered at pace, this investment has the potential to reduce homelessness, ease pressure on temporary accommodation and help more people access a safe, secure and affordable home.
Cllr Liam Robinson, Chair of the Local Government Association’s Inclusive Growth Committee, said:
Councils have long called for a sustained return to building genuinely affordable homes and stand ready to work with government to deliver the revival in social housebuilding.
The confirmed allocation of the first phase of the £39 billion fund and the increased Capacity to Build funding are positive steps to achieving this ambition.
Given the key role for councils in delivering these homes, it is crucial they remain at the heart of delivery. Mayors should work closely with local authorities in their areas to achieve the most from this money, with councils also having sustained access to preferential borrowing rates to support viability.
Notes to editors:
The Social and Affordable Homes Programme (SAHP) is a £39 billion investment programme over ten years. The programme has a target for at least 60% of homes delivered through it to be for Social Rent.
£9.58 billion is being allocated to 33 Strategic Partners outside of London, including housing associations and other providers, to support the delivery of 73,600 new social and affordable homes across England over the next ten years. Nearly two-thirds of homes delivered through these partnerships are expected to be for Social Rent. This is the first major wave of funding allocations under the programme. Further funding will be allocated over the lifetime of the programme.
Outside London, the Social and Affordable Homes Programme is administered by Homes England.
Section 106 (S106) agreements are, and will remain, an essential mechanism for delivering social and affordable housing in addition to grant-funded delivery, through the Social and Affordable Homes Programme
In 2025/26, councils received £1.61 billion in Right to Buy sales, all of which can now be retained and reinvested in new social and affordable homes.
The £46m ‘Capacity to Build’ funding forms a package of support to strengthen councils’ skills, capacity and capability to deliver and acquire new council homes. Building on the success of 2025-26, the £46m will fund the continuation of:
o   The Council Housebuilding Support Fund – delivered with Homes England, providing revenue funding for early-stage development activity to help councils bring forward ambitious bids to the SAHP;
o   The Council Housebuilding Support Service – delivered by the Local Government Association, providing bespoke no-cost support, advice and expertise to help councils deliver more homes;
An expansion to the Pathways to Planning graduate scheme – delivered by the Local Government Association, helping councils recruit and retain graduates in specialist housebuilding roles, including surveying and construction project management.
The Government has set out its long-term direction for the Social and Affordable Homes Programme, with more funding expected to flow directly to Established Mayoral Strategic Authorities (EMSAs) outside London as the programme progresses.
In allocating remaining funding, the government intends to prioritise Social Rent and council homes, alongside a continued focus on local decision-making and delivery.
Social Rent is the most affordable form of social housing. It is usually provided by councils or housing associations, with rents typically set well below private market rents. This makes it one of the most affordable housing options for people on low incomes.
Regional funding breakdown
For the following Established Mayoral Strategic Authorities outside of London, the estimated Strategic Partnership spend in each area is as follows:
o    Greater Manchester: £529m estimated spend to support c. 4,400 homes
o    West Midlands: £409m estimated spend to support c. 3,200 homes
o    North East: £445m estimated spend to support c. 3,400 homes
o    West Yorkshire: £441m estimated spend to support c. 4,000 homes
o    Liverpool City Region: £380m estimated spend to support c. 3,100 homes
o    South Yorkshire: £249m estimated spend to support c. 2,200 homes
Following the designation of four new Established Mayoral Strategic Authorities (EMSAs), they will now also be able to set the strategic direction of the Programme in their areas. Those EMSAs are: Cambridgeshire and Peterborough; East Midlands; West of England; York and North Yorkshire
Today’s announcement comes as the final National Planning Policy Framework is published last week that encourages a more diverse mix of housing, including more affordable homes for rural communities, and stricter rules to maximise social and affordable housing delivery on low-quality grey belt land.

Details
The Evaluation Task Force (ETF) is a joint HM Treasury (HMT) and Cabinet Office unit, set up in 2021 to place evaluation evidence at the heart of government decisions. The ETF jointly report to Cabinet Office Ministers and the Chief Secretary to the Treasury.
Following the delivery of our initial strategy, which has increased evaluation capability across government, improved transparency, and created a pipeline of new evaluations, this strategy marks a shift in our focus from verifying that evaluation happens to ensuring that robust evidence actively shapes government choices and drives better outcomes for the public.
The new strategy sets out the following priorities:
evaluating cross-government programmes;
strengthening governance and accountability;
building capability; and
driving innovation.
